h1: Aftertaste and finish and how to describe the length of a beer
title: Aftertaste and Finish in Beer | Craft Beer School
desc: How to describe a beer's aftertaste and finish: what length means, which compounds linger and simple words for short, medium and long finishes.
teaser: The beer is gone. The taste is not. How long it lingers and what it leaves tell you a lot about the beer.
standfirst: The finish is what a beer leaves behind after you swallow. Some vanish in a second. Others linger for half a minute. Learning to describe that length and character is one of the quickest ways to taste like a professional.
sections: Finish and aftertaste are slightly different

People use the words loosely, so it helps to split them. The finish is the last impression as you swallow: dry, sweet, bitter, clean or sticky. The aftertaste is what stays in your mouth and nose in the seconds afterwards. Its length is how long it lasts.

A crisp Pilsner might have a dry finish and a short, clean bitter aftertaste. An imperial stout might have a sweet, roasty finish with a long coffee and chocolate aftertaste. Both can be excellent. They are just built differently.

The simplest way to describe length is to count. Swallow, breathe out gently through your nose and count seconds until the flavour fades to almost nothing. Wine tasters have a word for this: a caudalie, one second of finish. Beer tasters rarely use the term, but the idea works.

  • Short: under about 5 seconds. Light lagers, many wheat beers.
  • Medium: roughly 5 to 15 seconds. Most pale ales, amber ales, brown ales.
  • Long: beyond about 15 seconds. Strong bitter IPAs, imperial stouts, barley wines.

These bands are a rough guide, not a standard. What matters is that you count the same way each time, so your notes stay comparable.
Bitterness, roast and alcohol linger longest

Different compounds hang around for different lengths of time. Hop bitterness from iso-alpha acids is famous for lingering, which is why a 70 IBU IPA can leave a bitter trace long after the sip. Roasted malt leaves a dry, coffee-like echo. Alcohol in a strong beer gives a warming finish that builds for a few seconds before it fades.

Sweetness usually fades faster, unless the beer is very sweet and full bodied. Aroma compounds can linger retronasally, especially resinous hops and dark fruit esters. Faults linger too: a metallic or astringent note can stay on the tongue well after the pleasant flavours have gone. Our guide on describing sweetness and dryness helps with the words for the finish itself.
Length is not the same as quality

In wine, a long finish is often praised. In beer it depends on the style. A long, sticky bitterness in a light lager is a fault. The beer is meant to clean up quickly and invite the next sip. A short, thin finish on an imperial stout is equally disappointing, because the style promises depth.

So describe what you find, then ask whether it suits the beer. A good finish is one that fits. A pleasant finish fades cleanly. An unpleasant one turns harsh, metallic or astringent as it goes.
Specific words beat smooth and nice

Vague words like nice or smooth do not help anyone. Try these instead:

  • Dry: little sweetness left, mouth feels clean.
  • Sweet or cloying: sugar and malt stay on the tongue.
  • Crisp: clean, quick, with a little bitterness or sharpness.
  • Lingering bitter: hop bitterness that stays and builds.
  • Warming: alcohol heat at the back of the throat.
  • Astringent: drying and puckering, like stewed tea.

Pair a word for character with a length: dry and short, sweet and long, bitter and medium. That two part note is enough to compare beers across months.

The same beer can finish differently from one pour to the next. Temperature is the biggest factor. Very cold beer mutes bitterness and sweetness, so the finish seems shorter and cleaner. As the beer warms towards 10 to 12 °C, more flavour comes through and the aftertaste lengthens. In Indian heat that change can happen within a single glass.

Carbonation matters too. A lively, well carbonated beer scrubs the palate and tends to finish crisper. The same beer gone flat often finishes sweeter and stickier. Glassware and food play their part as well. When you compare finishes, keep the temperature, glass and food the same, or your notes will measure the serving rather than the beer.
Why this helps at the bar

Describing the finish is one of the most useful things taproom staff can learn. A guest who says they hate bitter beer is often reacting to a long, harsh aftertaste rather than to bitterness itself. Steering them to a beer with a short, clean finish can win them over. Our guide on training taproom staff to taste covers how to build that habit across a team.

Pairing food works the same way. A long, bitter finish stands up to rich, fatty dishes. A short, crisp finish suits lighter food. Indian meals with layered spice often go best with beers that clean up quickly between bites.

Next time you have two different beers open, taste each and count the seconds of the aftertaste. Write the number and one word for its character. Do it with every beer for a week. By the end, you will be describing finishes that you would have missed entirely before.
faqs: What is the finish of a beer?
The finish is the last impression as you swallow, such as dry, sweet or bitter. The aftertaste is what lingers afterwards. Its length is how long it lasts.
How do you measure the length of a beer's finish?
Count the seconds from swallowing until the flavour fades. Under about 5 seconds is short, 5 to 15 is medium and longer than that is long.
Is a long finish always better?
No. It depends on the style. A crisp lager should finish short and clean, while an imperial stout is expected to linger.
